title: Rome: faith subjectively in intellect alone, yet will commands assent (Estius; 1 Corinthians 1:18; 2 Corinthians 10; Romans 4)
source_text: XXV. Quod spectat ad Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, communis Scholae Romanae doctrina est, fidem esse subjective in intellectu solo, non autem in voluntate. Nec tamen negant fidem ad voluntatem aliquo modo pertinere, & non intellectum solum, sed etiam voluntatem concurrere ad fidei actum. Quam rem explicat Guil. Estius in tertium Sententiarum, Distinctione 23. ubi dicit fidem partim intellectus esse, partim voluntatis; intellectus quidem tanquam subjecti, & propriae potentiae, quoniam ipsum credere, sive assentiri, qui est fidei actus, est cognitivae partis; voluntatis vero quia fides ab ea dependet, tanquam ab imperante & consentiente principio. Cum enim, inquit, humanae menti proprium sit ratione disceptare & examinare, sitne rebus propositis assentiendum, annon? Ea vero quae ad religionem pertinent talia fere sint quae rationis examen non admittant, utpote judicio humanae sapientiae ut plurimum improbabilia, ut docet Apostolus 1. Cor. 1. 18; profecto vel nunquam, vel raro intellectus noster rebus hujusmodi acquiesceret, nisi voluntatis imperio & inclinatione in assensum duceretur, & ut loquitur Apostolus, 2. Cor. 10. in captivitatem redigeretur in obsequium seu obedientiam Christi. Necessaria est igitur intellectui in credendo haec benigna voluntatis inclinatio, tum ut ad eas rationes se convertat quae fidem gignant nutriantque, vel saltem ostendant id quod creditur non esse absurdum, tum ut eas rejiciat quae assensum impedire aut remorari possint. Unde de Abrahamo dicitur Rom. 4. quod non consideravit corpus suum emortuum, &c. Est igitur assensus fidei ex consequenti etiam voluntatis actus, nimirum a voluntate imperatus, tum quoad ejus initium, tum quoad ejus continuationem.
pass_a_gloss: As for the Doctors of the Roman Church, the common doctrine of the Roman school is that faith is subjectively in the intellect alone, not in the will. Yet they do not deny that faith somehow belongs to the will, and that not intellect alone but also the will concurs to faith's act. William Estius explains this on the third book of the Sentences, Distinction 23, where he says faith is partly of intellect, partly of will; of intellect indeed as of the subject and proper power, because believing or assenting, which is faith's act, belongs to the cognitive part; but of will because faith depends on it as on a commanding and consenting principle. For since, he says, it is proper to the human mind to debate and examine by reason whether one should assent to things proposed or not, and yet things pertaining to religion are generally such as do not admit reason's examination — being for the most part improbable to human wisdom, as the Apostle teaches (1 Corinthians 1:18) — truly our intellect would never or rarely rest in such things unless led into assent by the will's command and inclination, and as the Apostle speaks (2 Corinthians 10) brought into captivity to the obedience of Christ. Necessary therefore for the intellect in believing is this kind inclination of the will, both that it turn to those reasons that beget and nourish faith or at least show what is believed is not absurd, and that it reject those that can hinder or delay assent. Whence of Abraham it is said (Romans 4) that he did not consider his own body as good as dead, etc. Therefore faith's assent is consequently also an act of the will — namely commanded by the will, both as to its beginning and as to its continuation.
pass_b_english: Rome seats faith subjectively in intellect alone, yet grants will concurs as commanding principle (Estius Sent. 3 dist. 23).
Religious objects rarely admit reason's exam (1 Corinthians 1:18); will must lead assent into Christ's obedience (2 Corinthians 10), as Abraham did not consider his dead body (Romans 4).
